source_refs.note: Chapter 21 exercise (PDF 184-185), solved: 10 MCQs keyed from the chapter's text, 7 short (Q7's 8 pairs separately), 9 long and 4 inquisitive questions with model answers. No answer key is printed. MCQ 10, Short Q5 and Long Q6 carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt: 1. Which of these are known for stimulating an immune response?
blocks.explanation: Antigens are the foreign molecules (e.g. on invading microbes) that T and B cells recognise and that stimulate the production of specific antibodies (21.3). Antibodies are the product of the response, not its stimulus.

blocks.prompt: 2. Which of the following is a part of the innate immune system?
blocks.explanation: Innate (inborn) immunity is the non-specific defence present at birth: the first line (skin, digestive and respiratory tracts) and second line. T cells, B cells and antibodies belong to acquired (specific) immunity (21.1, 21.3).

blocks.prompt: 3. Which of these is not involved in body’s non-specific defence?
blocks.explanation: NK cells, the complement system and inflammation are parts of the second (non-specific) line of defence; antibodies are made by B cells in the specific third line (21.2, 21.3).

blocks.prompt: 4. Skin offers an impenetrable barrier to microbes. It is categorized as;
blocks.explanation: Skin is part of the first line of defence, which acts against all microbes alike, so it is a non-specific defence (21.1, 21.2).

blocks.prompt: 5. What is the difference between B cells and T cells?

options.text: B cells make antibodies, and T cells destroy infected cells
B cells and T cells do the same work
B cells attack germs directly, and T cells make antibodies
B cells fight germs in body fluids, and T cells work inside cells

blocks.explanation: B cells give plasma cells that secrete antibodies (antibody-mediated immunity); cytotoxic T cells recognise and destroy infected or cancer cells (cell-mediated immunity) (21.3.2). T cells attack infected cells from outside, not inside them, so (d) is not accurate.

blocks.prompt: 6. How do the neutrophils kill microbes?
blocks.explanation: Neutrophils kill pathogens by phagocytosis (engulfing and digesting), by releasing anti-microbial chemicals, and by releasing a network of DNA fibres (21.2.1). Of the options, only (a) is correct.

blocks.prompt: 7. Which group of chemicals is involved in inflammatory response?
blocks.explanation: Infected or injured cells release histamines and prostaglandins, which widen blood vessels and make capillaries leaky, causing redness, swelling and warmth (21.2.3). Pyrogens cause fever.

blocks.prompt: 8. Which type of white blood cell is responsible for producing antibodies?
blocks.explanation: On meeting its antigen, a B cell divides into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies (21.3.1, 21.3.2).

blocks.prompt: 9. What types of drug are not prescribed to a recipient of organ-transplantation?
blocks.explanation: The recipient's T and B cells may attack the transplanted organ, so doctors give drugs that suppress the immune system; drugs that strengthen immunity would increase rejection (21.3.3).

blocks.prompt: 10. Cell-mediated immunity works best against;

options.text: Viruses infected cells and toxic molecules
Virus infected cells and cancer cells

blocks.explanation: Cell-mediated immunity, by cytotoxic T cells, kills virus-infected and abnormal (cancer) cells. Toxic molecules are inactivated by antibodies (antibody-mediated immunity) (21.3.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (a) is printed "Viruses infected cells"; it should read "Virus-infected cells" (as in option (c)).

blocks.prompt: 1. Define the roles of the different types of T cells.
blocks.explanation:
1. Helper T cells: initiate the immune response; activate cell-mediated and antibody-mediated immunity.
2. Cytotoxic T cells: break (kill) cells infected by microbes, and cancer cells.
3. Inducer T cells: supervise the development (maturation) of T cells in the thymus.
4. Suppressor T cells: terminate (shut down) the immune response.

blocks.prompt: 2. Skin is an important component of our defence system. Comment.
blocks.explanation: Skin is the first line of defence. Its epidermis is 10-30 cells thick; the outer stratum corneum cells are filled with tough keratin and are continuously shed and replaced, making an impenetrable barrier. Oil and sweat glands lower the surface pH to 3-5, which inhibits microbial growth, and sweat contains lysozyme, which digests bacterial cell walls.

blocks.prompt: 3. State how the digestive and respiratory tracts play a role in body’s defence.
blocks.explanation:
Digestive tract: lysozyme in saliva kills many bacteria in food; strong stomach acid and protein-digesting enzymes of the intestine kill more.
Respiratory tract: ciliated epithelium of the nasal cavity traps bacteria; cells of bronchi and bronchioles secrete sticky mucus that traps microbes, and cilia sweep the mucus up to be swallowed.

blocks.prompt: 4. How the natural killer cells play role in body’s defence?
blocks.explanation: Natural killer cells are germ-killer lymphocytes of the second line of defence. They do not attack microbes; they detect body cells infected with viruses and release perforins, which make a pore in the target cell membrane; water rushes in and the cell swells and bursts. They also detect and kill cancer cells before they form a tumour.

blocks.prompt: 5. Define pyrogens and state their effect of hypothalamus.
blocks.explanation: Pyrogens are chemicals released by macrophages when they attack invading microbes. They travel in the blood to the hypothalamus (the body's thermostat) and stimulate it to raise the body's core temperature above the normal 37°C, causing fever, which hinders microbial reproduction and speeds up neutrophils and macrophages.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question is printed "their effect of hypothalamus"; it should read "their effect on hypothalamus".

blocks.prompt: 6. What do you mean by autoimmune diseases?
blocks.explanation: Autoimmune diseases result when the immune system cannot distinguish body cells from foreign materials, so it attacks and destroys the body's own cells and tissues. Examples: myasthenia gravis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis and type I diabetes.

blocks.prompt: 1. Describe the role of macrophages and neutrophils in killing bacteria.
blocks.explanation:
Macrophages and neutrophils are germ-killer cells of the blood, the most important part of the non-specific second line of defence; they patrol the bloodstream and attack invaders.
Macrophages:
1. Develop from monocytes (white blood cells) that enter the tissues.
2. Ingest a bacterium by endocytosis (phagocytosis) and kill it with lysozyme enzymes.
3. Some are fixed in organs (lungs, liver, spleen, brain); most patrol blood, lymph and interstitial fluid.
4. In inflammation they migrate to the site, engulf microbes and clean up dead microbes, cells and debris.
5. They release pyrogens (causing fever) and produce proteins that activate helper T cells, linking to specific immunity.
6. They destroy antibody-coated antigens.
Neutrophils (a type of white blood cell) kill pathogens by three methods:
1. Phagocytosis: engulfing and digesting them.
2. Releasing soluble anti-microbial chemicals onto them.
3. Releasing a network of DNA fibres that binds and kills bacteria.
They migrate in large numbers to inflamed tissue; dead neutrophils with tissue cells and pathogens form pus.
These cells do not attack the body's own cells, which carry self-proteins.

blocks.prompt: 2. Explain how the proteins of the complement system kill bacteria and how the interferons inhibit the ability of viruses to infect cells.
blocks.explanation:
Complement system:
1. More than a dozen different proteins, made in the liver, circulate in the blood in an inactive state.
2. On meeting a microbe they are activated in sequence: the first activates the second, and so on (a cascade).
3. The final five proteins form a membrane-attack complex (MAC) in the plasma membrane of the microbe.
4. The MAC punctures the membrane; fluids and salts move in, and the microbe swells and bursts.
5. Some antibodies bound to antigens also activate complement (in antibody-mediated immunity).
Interferons:
1. Protective proteins released by virus-infected cells; they belong to the cytokines, which carry messages between cells.
2. They reach nearby cells and make them enhance their anti-viral defences, so viruses cannot easily infect them.
3. They also activate other immune cells such as natural killer cells and macrophages, which destroy infected cells.
4. More interferons are released during fever.

blocks.prompt: 3. Inflammation is one of the most generalized nonspecific defences. How?
blocks.explanation:
Inflammation is a general response to any infection or injury, whatever the microbe:
1. Infected or injured cells release chemical signals: histamines and prostaglandins.
2. These cause local widening of blood vessels, increasing capillary blood flow to the site.
3. Capillaries become more permeable, so fluid leaks out: redness, swelling and warmth (inflammation).
4. The heat makes the site unfavourable for microbial growth, promotes healing and raises the mobility of white blood cells.
5. More phagocytes (macrophages and neutrophils) migrate from the blood into the inflamed tissue and engulf microbes.
6. Monocytes arrive and release chemicals that kill microbes; then macrophages clean up dead microbes, cells and debris (pus is dead neutrophils, broken tissue cells and dead pathogens).
Because it is triggered by any damage, acts at once against all kinds of microbes and is often strong enough to stop their spread, it is one of the most generalized non-specific defences.

blocks.prompt: 4. How are monocytes, T-cells and B-cells the components of the immune system?
blocks.explanation:
The immune system is not in one place; it is made of white blood cells that arise in the bone marrow, circulate in blood and lymph, and are found in lymph nodes, spleen, liver, thymus and bone marrow. Its three main kinds are monocytes, T cells and B cells (T and B cells are lymphocytes).
1. Monocytes: WBCs produced in lymphoid tissues; they enter interstitial fluid and mature into macrophages that phagocytose microbes and produce proteins that activate helper T cells. Others become phagocytes in liver, spleen and lymph nodes, clearing debris and helping repair tissue.
2. T cells: develop from bone-marrow stem cells and mature in the thymus, where they learn to identify antigens; tens of millions of kinds, each recognising one antigen. Four kinds: helper (initiate the response), cytotoxic (kill infected cells), inducer (supervise T-cell development), suppressor (end the response). They carry out cell-mediated immunity.
3. B cells: develop and mature in the bone marrow, then circulate in blood and lymph; each recognises a particular antigen. On meeting it a B cell divides into plasma cells that secrete antibodies, marking the antigen for destruction (antibody-mediated immunity); some become memory B cells.
Together they recognise specific invaders, destroy them and remember them, so they form the specific third line of defence.

blocks.prompt: 5. Differentiate the two types of acquired immunity (active and passive immunity).
blocks.explanation: Acquired (specific) immunity develops during growth and is of two types. In active immunity the body itself prepares antibodies against antigens; it may be natural (after natural exposure to antigens, the most effective form) or artificial (vaccination with weakened antigens that stimulate antibodies against the real ones). In passive immunity the individual is given ready-made antibodies to combat specific microbes; it is short-lived.

rows: Body makes its own antibodies against antigens
e.g. injected antibodies against specific microbes

blocks.prompt: 6. Describe the roles T-cells in cell-mediated immunity.
blocks.explanation:
When a macrophage engulfs a microbe it produces special proteins; helper T cells recognise them through their receptors and are activated. They start cell-mediated immunity, carried out by T cells against virus-infected and cancer cells. Events:
1. Proliferation: activated helper T cells produce T cell growth factor, which makes all types of T cells multiply into large clones that recognise the antigen.
2. Activation: helper T cells secrete a second factor that attracts macrophages to the site of infection.
3. Induction: helper T cells activate inducer T cells in the thymus, which trigger maturation of lymphocytes into T cells.
4. Attack: receptors on cytotoxic T cells recognise and bind infected body cells and disrupt (puncture) their membranes, so the cells burst (same mechanism as natural killer cells).
5. Suppression: suppressor T cells multiply more slowly; after 1-2 weeks they are numerous enough to shut down the cytotoxic response.
6. Memory: a population of helper and cytotoxic T cells (memory cells) persists, probably for life, giving a rapid response if the same microbe returns.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question is printed "Describe the roles T-cells"; it should read "Describe the roles of T-cells".

blocks.prompt: 7. Describe the role of B-cells in antibody-mediated immunity.
blocks.explanation:
Activated helper T cells also start antibody-mediated (humoral) immunity, a second, stronger defence. B cells do not attack antigens directly; they mark them for destruction and inactivate toxic molecules. Events:
1. Proliferation: each B cell binds its antigen through B receptor proteins on its surface; helper T cells bind to these antigen-bound B cells and release proteins that make them divide into many plasma cells.
2. Differentiation and secretion: plasma cells stop dividing and make more B receptor proteins, which are secreted as antibodies; a great number are released in a few days.
3. Attack: antibodies mark antigens for destruction by (i) complement: activating complement proteins that make holes in the antigen cell so it swells and bursts; (ii) macrophages, which recognise, ingest and break antibody-coated antigens; (iii) killer cells, which have receptors for antibody-coated antigens and kill them.
4. Suppression: after several weeks suppressor T cells shut down the antibody response.
5. Memory: some cells of the clone persist as memory B cells and give a rapid secondary response to the same antigen later; vaccines work by forming such memory cells.
Antibody structure: Y-shaped, two heavy and two light chains joined by disulphide bridges; variable regions form specific antigen-binding sites.

blocks.prompt: 8. Define allergies. Correlate the symptoms of allergies with the release of histamines.
blocks.explanation:
Allergies are the hypersensitivity of the immune system to weak antigens (allergens) that do not cause an immune response in most people, e.g. dust, moulds, pollen, cat dander, certain foods and some medicines (penicillin).
Mechanism and symptoms:
1. After exposure to an allergen some people make E-antibodies.
2. E-antibodies bind to mast cells (in connective tissue around blood vessels).
3. On the next exposure the allergen reacts with these antibodies, and the mast cells release histamines.
4. Histamines start an inflammatory response: dilation of blood vessels gives redness and warmth; leakage of fluid from capillaries gives swelling, a runny nose and watery eyes; irritation gives sneezing and itching (skin rashes).
5. In some people a massive histamine release causes anaphylactic shock, in which swelling makes breathing difficult; it can be life-threatening.
So the symptoms are the effects of histamine. Treatment: antihistamine drugs block histamines and give temporary relief; desensitization (injecting allergen extracts) makes G-antibodies that destroy the allergen before it reaches the E-antibodies.

blocks.prompt: 9. How are T-cells and B-cells related to transplant rejections?
blocks.explanation:
1. Every person's cells carry a particular set of self-proteins, like molecular fingerprints; one's own T and B cells recognise them and attack only foreign cells.
2. In an organ transplant, the self-proteins on the donor organ may not match the recipient's.
3. The recipient's T cells (cytotoxic) then attack the cells of the transplanted organ, and B cells produce antibodies against its proteins. This is transplant rejection.
Prevention:
1. Choosing a donor whose self-proteins match as closely as possible: identical twin (100% match) > sibling > parent > unrelated donor (chance of match about 1 in 100,000-200,000).
2. Drugs that suppress the recipient's immune system (these also reduce the ability to fight infections).
3. Monoclonal antibodies to destroy the T cells that attack the transplant.
4. Stem cells to make a new immune system that recognises the transplant as self.

blocks.prompt: 1. Rationalize the inflammatory response in arthritis as an example of a misdirected immune response.
blocks.explanation: Inflammation is meant to fight infection or injury: chemical signals widen vessels, phagocytes gather and microbes are destroyed, after which it stops. In arthritis, inflammation occurs in the joints in the absence of any infection or injury. In rheumatoid arthritis the immune system cannot distinguish self from foreign and forms antibodies against the cartilaginous tissue of the joints (an autoimmune disease). The resulting inflammation (swelling, pain, warmth) and the chemicals of attacking cells damage the body's own joints instead of microbes. So a protective response is aimed at the wrong target, the body itself: a misdirected immune response.

blocks.prompt: 2. Justify why the physicians prescribe antipyretic drugs, when fever is a nonspecific defence against microbial infections.
blocks.explanation: A moderate fever is useful: pyrogens from macrophages make the hypothalamus raise body temperature, which hinders bacterial and viral reproduction, kills temperature-sensitive microbes and speeds up neutrophils and macrophages. But the benefit has a limit. Temperatures above about 103°F (39.4°C) are considered dangerous and above about 105°F (40.5°C) are often fatal, because very high heat harms the body's own cells, enzymes and brain. High fever also causes discomfort, dehydration and weakness (and fits in small children, beyond the chapter). So physicians give antipyretics to keep the temperature within a safe range and relieve the patient, while the infection itself is treated with other drugs (e.g. antibiotics) and the immune system continues to work.

blocks.prompt: 3. Justify why physicians prescribe antihistamine therapy to the patients of runny nose or skin rashes.
blocks.explanation: Runny nose and skin rashes are usually allergic responses. In an allergy, E-antibodies bound to mast cells react with the allergen (dust, pollen, certain foods, medicines) and the mast cells release histamines. Histamines cause dilation of blood vessels and leakage of fluid, producing a runny nose, sneezing, itching, redness and swelling of the skin (rashes). The harmless allergen is not the real problem; the symptoms are caused by histamine. Antihistamine drugs block histamines, so these effects stop and the patient gets (temporary) relief. They do not cure the allergy; avoiding the allergen or desensitization is needed for longer control.

blocks.prompt: 4. Describe the discovery of monoclonal antibodies and justify how this accomplishment revolutionized many aspects of biological research.
blocks.explanation:
Background: only a small part of an antigen, the determinant, fits an antibody's binding site. Antibodies that attach to different determinants of one antigen are polyclonal; antibodies that attach to only one determinant are monoclonal.
Discovery: Cesar Milstein and George Kohler (Nobel Prize, 1984) mixed antibody-producing plasma cells with cancer cells called myelomas. Some fused cells, called hybridomas, grew and divided in culture: they used the plasma-cell genes to make one specific antibody and the myeloma genes to divide endlessly. So rapidly growing hybridoma cells produced large amounts of one pure (monoclonal) antibody.
Why revolutionary:
1. Large amounts of a single, highly specific antibody became available, which normal plasma cells cannot give because they do not divide in culture.
2. Purification: they can pick out and purify specific molecules from complex mixtures; interferon was purified this way.
3. Medicine: they act as vehicles for delivering specific therapies; research is under way to target radioactive monoclonal antibodies to antigens found only on cancer cells, killing them selectively.
4. Transplants: monoclonal antibodies are used to destroy the T cells that attack a transplanted organ.
5. (Beyond the chapter:) they are the basis of many diagnostic tests (e.g. pregnancy and disease tests) and of identifying and locating specific proteins in cells and tissues in research.
